clue.text: Intended I should go in for run in the country

indicators.note: going in for something means taking its place, so one letter stands in where another was

parts.note: the country is taken as a European nation
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone planned to stand in for a runner competing for their country.
explanation.walkthrough: In FRANCE the R (run) is swapped out for I.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's betrothed partner is his intended, an old-fashioned noun for the person someone plans to marry.

clue.text: Plot to destroy world with beef

indicators.note: destroying the words breaks them up so their letters can be rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
joins the two words of fodder

explanation.surface: A conspiracy to wreck the planet with meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' reads as a conspiracy; it is a patch of garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot is a small piece of ground, and a garden bed planted with blooms is one such patch.

clue.text: One way to uphold two articles, though one rejects thirty-nine

indicators.note: in a down clue, holding something up means sitting beneath it, so these pieces come after

parts.note: the indefinite article and the definite article
I is the Roman numeral for one
St is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A churchman supports two Anglican articles while rejecting the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Thirty-Nine Articles are the doctrinal statements of the Church of England; someone who rejects all of them, including belief in God, is a nonbeliever.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone denying God's existence would reject every one of the Church of England's founding doctrinal statements.

clue.text: Remember to go round for babysitting

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to bring back into memory
second meaning, read literally: to visit (call) in order to look after (mind)

explanation.surface: A reminder that someone promised to pop over and look after the children.
explanation.walkthrough: Read word by word, the phrase means to visit for the purpose of minding a child.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to recall something, and its words literally describe visiting a house to look after a child.

clue.text: Confused roarings in place full of soldiers

indicators.note: confused letters are jumbled out of their proper sequence

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A barracks echoes with a muddle of shouting.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified post or town where a body of troops is stationed is named after that body of troops.

clue.text: Tree hit by gunfire in military town

parts.note: the alder is a tree
something hit by gunfire has been shot

explanation.surface: A tree is damaged during firing practice at an army base.
explanation.walkthrough: Aldershot in Hampshire is known as the home of the British Army.
explanation.definitionFit: This Hampshire town has been a major British Army garrison since the 1850s, the home of the army.

clue.text: Stone killer of an assassin once

definitions.meaning: second meaning: Jack ..., who shot Lee Harvey Oswald in 1963

explanation.surface: A rock was the weapon that killed a hired murderer long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: Oswald assassinated President Kennedy and was himself shot two days later by nightclub owner Jack Ruby.
explanation.definitionFit: It names a precious red gem and also the Dallas nightclub owner who shot Kennedy's assassin.

clue.text: Pupil's trick to conceal low grades

indicators.note: concealing something means hiding it inside, so one piece is wrapped round the other

parts.note: a stunt is a trick or feat
D and E are low marks in a grading scale

explanation.surface: A schoolchild schemes to hide bad marks from their parents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pupil's' reads as possessive but is 'pupil is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil is someone being taught at school or college, which is a learner by another name.

clue.text: Note a hesitant expression from prophet

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for note
taken as written
a hum is a hesitant noise, as in hum and haw

explanation.surface: A seer, unsure, makes a noncommittal noise.
explanation.definitionFit: He is one of the twelve minor biblical seers, with a short Old Testament book bearing his name.

clue.text: Wooden bar gives security

definitions.meaning: first meaning: one of the small wooden crosspieces on top of cricket stumps
second meaning: money pledged to secure a prisoner's release

explanation.surface: A timber bolt keeps a door safe.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, two small wooden pieces rest on top of the stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: It names a crosspiece resting on cricket stumps and also the sum pledged to get an accused person released before trial.

clue.text: Hope destroyed, distress disoriented this tragic figure

indicators.note: a destroyed word is broken up and its letters rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something disoriented has lost its direction, here running the opposite way

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or distress

explanation.surface: A doomed heroine, her hopes ruined and her mind wandering in grief.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a fair sketch of the heroine herself: hope gone, distracted by sorrow.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's beloved goes mad and drowns, making her one of Shakespeare's most pitiable doomed characters.

clue.text: Hard copper retired, rejected as corrupt

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the string so far is read from its end

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
someone who has retired for the night is in bed

explanation.surface: A tough policeman, now retired, was turned down as crooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'retired' paint a former policeman, but they give a metal symbol and a word for gone to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To debauch someone is to lead them into immoral excess, so the verb means to deprave or corrupt.

clue.text: Like letters I put in early post, perhaps

indicators.note: a letter put in goes inside the other letters
perhaps marks the words as one possible arrangement of letters, not the final one

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone describes posting their correspondence in time for the first collection.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to or written as correspondence, as in a novel told through a series of missives.

clue.text: Join to appear sound

indicators.note: sound tells the solver to go by how a word is pronounced

parts.note: to appear is to seem

explanation.surface: Signing up in order to look healthy and fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like the adjective meaning healthy; it signals the pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: A seam is the line where two pieces of fabric are stitched together, a noun for a join.

clue.text: Still nothing changed

definitions.meaning: second meaning: everything identical, read literally

explanation.surface: Everything stays exactly as it was.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like motionless, which matches the surface; it means nevertheless.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase works as an adverb meaning nevertheless and literally describes everything remaining identical.

clue.text: Early, possibly Arab., book brought back

indicators.note: brought back means returned, so the letters are read from the far end

parts.note: an Arab is one example of a Semite, which 'possibly' signals
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: An early edition of an Arabic book, perhaps, has been returned.
explanation.walkthrough: Semitic peoples include Arabs and Jews, so an Arab is a Semite.
explanation.definitionFit: Betimes is an archaic adverb for in good time or at an early hour, a literary synonym.

clue.text: One could appear very sorry if it suited one

definitions.text: One could appear very sorry if it suited one

parts.words: One could appear very sorry if it suited one
parts.note: surface reading: a person would seem contrite if it were convenient
setter's reading: if a suit were made of this coarse fabric, worn traditionally as a sign of penitence

explanation.walkthrough: 'Suited' reads as convenient but means clothed. Wearing rough garments with ashes on the head was the biblical sign of mourning or repentance.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse fabric made from hessian was traditionally worn as a public mark of grief or remorse, alongside ashes.

clue.text: Look to include junior officer in joint summit

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: the hip is a joint of the body

indicators.note: in places the built-up piece inside the word for joint

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: A command to check that a young officer is part of a combined peak meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint summit' reads as a shared conference; joint is the hip and summit alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a hill is a summit, the highest point that a climber reaches.

clue.text: Half as much rye as one can get into bags?

definitions.text: Half as much rye as one can get into bags?

parts.words: Half as much rye as one can get into bags?
parts.note: surface reading: a puzzle about the capacity of grain sacks
setter's reading: bags are trousers, which have two pockets, and the nursery rhyme Sing a Song of Sixpence speaks of a quantity of rye that fills one

explanation.walkthrough: Bags is old British slang for trousers. The nursery rhyme begins 'Sing a song of sixpence, a ... of rye'.
explanation.definitionFit: The amount one trouser pouch can hold is half what both together hold, and the rhyme measures rye this way.

clue.text: Make very short note for monastic head

parts.note: to do is to make, as in do a drawing
mini means very small or short
C is a musical note

explanation.surface: A brief memo is drafted for the abbot.
explanation.walkthrough: St Dominic founded the order of friars named after him, so he heads a religious order.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint Dominic founded the Dominican order of friars, making him the founding leader of a religious order.

clue.text: Blossom lovely in this part of town

parts.note: may is hawthorn blossom
fair means lovely or beautiful

explanation.surface: Pretty flowers bloom in a smart district.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayfair is an expensive district of London's West End.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a wealthy district of London's West End, named after a fair once held there each spring.

clue.text: Some bought it, an iceberg doing for this

definitions.text: Some bought it, an iceberg doing for this

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is wanted, sitting inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the words bought, it, an and iceberg

explanation.surface: Many passengers died when an iceberg finished off a famous ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bought it' is slang for died; the whole clue describes the ship's sinking while also hiding its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The White Star liner sank in 1912 after striking an iceberg, with great loss of life.

clue.text: More than anyone else, mean to read a Sterne novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are given a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A stingy reader picks up an eighteenth-century book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book by Laurence Sterne; it is the anagram signal. Near is an old word for stingy.
explanation.definitionFit: Near can mean tight-fisted, so its superlative describes someone stingier than everyone else.

clue.text: Plays, using two eyes alternately

indicators.note: alternately means taking every other letter, skipping the ones between

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: A performer plays a part by winking with each eye in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To toy with something is to play or trifle with it, so the verb forms match.

clue.text: Theme to play on banjo endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly means the final letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
to pick is to pluck the strings of a banjo

explanation.surface: A tune to strum over and over on a banjo.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is the subject of a talk or essay, which is what a theme is.

clue.text: Behave responsibly and start to play the wise man

parts.note: the first part of a stage play is Act One
a sage is a wise man

explanation.surface: Advice to grow up and take on the role of a wise elder.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole phrase is re-split: an idiom first, then the opening of a play followed by a word for a wise man.
explanation.definitionFit: To behave in a manner suitable for one's years is the meaning of this idiom urging maturity.

clue.text: Profanity once heard on tennis court

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a curse or swear word
second meaning: the Tennis Court pledge sworn by French deputies in 1789

explanation.surface: A player once swore loudly on court.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a tantrum at Wimbledon; in fact it is the 1789 Tennis Court vow of the French Revolution.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a swear word and a solemn promise, like the one French revolutionaries swore at a royal tennis hall.

clue.text: For patriarch, it's sinful putting money first instead of last

indicators.text: putting money first instead of last
indicators.note: the instruction moves one letter from the end of a word to its front

parts.note: evil means sinful
L stands for pound, the British unit of money

explanation.surface: Someone claims a father figure is wicked for valuing cash above all.
explanation.walkthrough: The L ending the word for sinful moves to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the third son of Jacob in Genesis and founder of one of the twelve tribes of Israel.

clue.text: Identify unpleasant smell in inactive substance

parts.note: to place someone is to recognise or identify them
BO is body odour

explanation.surface: Someone recognises a nasty whiff coming from an inert chemical.
explanation.definitionFit: A dummy pill given in medical trials has no pharmacological effect, so it is a dummy medicine with no action.

clue.text: Thief taking small piece in bag?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Cockney rhyming slang for a thief
second meaning: a fragment of dried leaf packed in a teabag

explanation.surface: A burglar lifts a small item and stuffs it in his sack.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cockney rhyming slang a phrase rhymes with the word it replaces, so this one stands for thief. The question mark flags the playful second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang turns thief into this phrase, and literally it is a scrap of the brewing plant found in a teabag.

clue.text: My word! what a suitable place for a coastal road!

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise
a niche is a suitable or comfortable place for someone

explanation.surface: An admiring exclamation at a spot ideal for building a seaside highway.
explanation.definitionFit: A corniche is a road cut along a cliff or the side of a mountain, especially one by the sea.

clue.text: Pulse is fast — endlessly unwell

indicators.note: endlessly means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting
ill means unwell

explanation.surface: A patient's heartbeat is racing and they can't stop feeling sick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' and 'fast' suggest a racing heartbeat, but pulse is a food and fast is a religious season.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are the edible seeds of legumes such as beans and peas, and a lentil is one kind.
